data.title: Kamala Harris urges a 'too big to rig' turnout for the midterms and tees off on Trump
data.description:
Kamala Harris urges a 'too big to rig' turnout for the midterms and tees off on Trump

BILL BARROW
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 3:14 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Election 2026 Georgia Senate

1 of 3
Former Vice President Kamala Harris shakes hands on the rope line during a campaign event on the campus of Clark Atlanta University, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart) (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)

ATLANTA (AP) — Two years after Kamala Harris lost the presidential election to Donald Trump, she still delights Democratic donors and activists with jabs against him, saying the Republican is "callous, corrupt and incompetent" and calling him the "decorator in chief" for his White House renovations and gold adornments.

But the former vice president also has plenty to say about what her party, the electorate and the country should do next as she also considers whether to run again.

"This is the moment where we turn that anger into action," Harris said more than once during a busy schedule in the final stretch of the midterm campaign.

Advertisement

Harris campaigned for candidates across seven states, ending with a recent two-day visit to Georgia. It was, in parts, the kind of nostalgic tour seen from Barack Obama and Bill Clinton — two-term presidents whose last campaigns are behind them — and the barnstorming from potential future contenders such as Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky or U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

As the first Black woman elected to nationwide office, Harris urged fellow Black Americans to "honor the ancestors" with their votes but she also has become unapologetically "transactional" by demanding more from politicians.

Harris, a California senator before joining Joe Biden on the 2020 ticket, also pushed fellow Democrats to govern aggressively and she called for "structural work" that she said was necessary to reinvigorate American democracy: U.S. Supreme Court expansion, statehood for the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, and reconsideration of the Electoral College.

"I think she's hitting all the right notes," said Melinda Johnson, a retired nurse who attended a Fulton County Democratic Party fundraising gala that Harris headlined in Atlanta.

Harris made it to early presidential primary states, including Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan. She also went to Mississippi, not exactly a hotbed of presidential politics, on behalf of U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom.

"The South is in play," she said. "When Democrats invest in the South, we can win in the South."

In Georgia, Harris delved into civil rights history as she accused the U.S. Supreme Court of "backdoor racism" with its decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and allow Republicans to redraw boundaries for congressional districts that now elect nonwhite lawmakers.

"Ruthlessness" is key, she said at the Democratic dinner in Atlanta. "Not ruthlessness in the sense of cruelty … but in our willingness to use our power to deliver on our commitments." Democrats, she said, "can no longer let process stand in the way of progress."

Throughout her stops, Harris nodded implicitly at her loss to Trump.

"You know we've been spending the last year and a half, so many of us, going through a range of emotions," she told students. "Anger, depression, sadness, frustration, a sense of helplessness and powerlessness."

Warning that Trump could try to meddle in Tuesday's election, she echoed one of the president's own mantras to encourage people to vote.

"In this case," she said at Atlanta's Elizabeth Baptist Church, "we just need to turn out in really large numbers that would be too big to rig."

data.title: Gulf nations scramble to prevent Iran war from again hitting their doorstep
data.description:
Persian Gulf scrambling to prevent Iran war from again hitting its doorstep

Rachel Chason and Suzan Haidamous, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Sat, October 31, 2026 at 9:02 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

MANAMA, Bahrain - The looming possibility of U.S. strikes on Iran has been met with weary nervousness in the Persian Gulf, as Gulf officials double down on efforts to break through a U.S.-Iran impasse that they know will leave their region vulnerable.

Publicly and privately, leaders in Persian Gulf nations, which bore the brunt of Iranian retaliation because they are home to U.S. bases, are calling for de-escalation as concerns about President Donald Trump's war plans grow. Mediators from Qatar arrived in Tehran on Friday as part of the efforts to negotiate an end to the war, according to a person briefed on the talks, who described the trip as a "last-ditch effort to broker an interim deal between Iran and the U.S." that was happening "in coordination with the U.S."

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

Trump has seemed open to a deal - but also to resuming strikes, according to a separate official briefed on the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation. Vice President JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and envoy, have been pushing for a deal, the official added, as others - including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth - appear opposed to it.

"The next two days will be crucial in determining how the situation unfolds," said an Iranian official, who like some others interviewed for this story spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation. The Americans, they added, are "seeking a positive breakthrough" ahead of the midterm elections.

A White House official said in a statement that the United States is "in a very strong position," pointing to U.S. gains in the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's struggling economy.

"Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."

Trump, the official said, "has great relationships with all of our Gulf partners, and the U.S. has been in regular contact with all of our regional allies since before Operation Epic Fury."

On the ground in the Gulf, there is fear and fatigue as the region once again braces for the possibility of drone and missile strikes after months of relative quiet. In Bahrain, an island nation of 1.69 million that has hosted the U.S. Fifth Fleet for more than 30 years and was targeted by hundreds of Iranian drones and missiles, signs of the previous phases of escalation are still obvious.

Damage to equipment and infrastructure at the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Manama, which analysts have put in the hundreds of millions, is evident even from the highway. Restaurants and shops long frequented by military members and their families, the vast majority of whom have been evacuated, are empty. Bahrainis said they have been watching the news nervously.

"People are expecting something will happen. We don't want it, but we expect it," said Taha Bhutto, 37, a manager at a car dealership who said that during the first months of the war, he watched as drones and missiles flew overhead.

At a supermarket, where prices have surged because of supply chain disruptions linked to diminished traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the store manager said he is stockpiling food and water for his family in case of an escalation. At a hair salon, where business has plummeted during the war, stylists said they are praying that fighting doesn't kick off again.

Many said that their perception of the United States had changed over the course of the war - and that they had believed the Fifth Fleet base would protect them but were disappointed to instead find it becoming a vulnerability.

"Trump's decisions have affected the whole region," said Ibrahim, a manager at a supermarket in Bahrain. "We should not have been brought into this chaos. We didn't do anything."

Ibrahim, who spoke on the condition that only his first name be used because of concerns about criticizing a Bahraini ally, said that everyone here knows that "a dangerous moment" has arrived.

"We know that any outcome will be disastrous - and felt most here," he said.

Concerns are especially intense surrounding the targeting of civilian infrastructure in the Gulf, which officials fear could be at risk if Trump follows through on his reported plans to resume attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. Speaking at an event Wednesday at the Middle East Institute, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) called those plans, which he said he had been briefed on and included strikes on civilian infrastructure, "insane" and bound to lead to a "devastating escalation."

"This is the worst scenario for the region," said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, an Emirati analyst and a retired political science professor. "The chances for a strike after the election - or maybe even before it - appear to be growing by the day."

The United Arab Emirate's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday released a statement saying that there was a "need to intensify diplomatic efforts" and "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to contain tensions. Earlier in the week, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called on Gulf nations to form a security pact that includes Iran and Iraq, saying that there has been a "terrible cost" to antagonizing and excluding Iran.

Since the war began, Gulf nations - which have long fallen under the U.S. security umbrella - have been bolstering their defenses by ramping up purchases from the U.S. but also looking to other partners, including Turkey and South Korea.

Shortages of ballistic missile interceptors (Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense or THAAD) could leave Gulf nations vulnerable, said Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

But in terms of the lower layers of air defense - the counter-drone systems - Vidal said the Gulf states have a "greater menu of available options" than at the beginning of the conflict in February 2026.

One thing that is unclear, he noted, is how many ballistic missiles Iran still has in its arsenal.

"The Gulf states are in a lose-lose situation," said Thomas Juneau, a professor at the University of Ottawa whose work focuses on Middle East security issues, noting that global interceptor stocks are running low.

Interception rates during the first waves of strikes were higher than anticipated, he said, but Gulf defenses still cannot stop every possible hit.

"It's impossible for them to be 100 percent effective," he said, adding that the geography of a country as big as Saudi Arabia - which is also facing attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants - poses a special challenge.

"It is a fantasy to think they could defend it all."

data.title: FBI questions donors as 2 Dan Sullivans compete in Alaska Senate race
data.description:
FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's home town as Alaska Senate inquiry widens

JOSHUA GOODMAN and JIM MUSTIAN
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 4:18 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI on Friday began reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation over the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.

An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician.

The FBI visit came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion.

Advertisement

Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for "throwing his hat in the ring." Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been "misled" about which candidate he was supporting.

"I don't feel like I've been misled at all," Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would "let him waste his time trying to track me down."

"I don't think there's any confusion," he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. "Everybody knows who the incumbent is."

Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."

The developments come just days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied any involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator.

She said she was "deeply offended" by the allegations, which she called "garbage" and part of a "smear campaign" to suppress turnout on the eve of the election.

"I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race," she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press reporter Becky Bohrer contributed reporting from Juneau, Alaska.

data.title: Criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate in Alaska
data.description:
Trump administration accelerates criminal probe into Alaska Senate race

By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Frandino
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 2:06 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Frandino

WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, officials said on Friday, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday's midterm elections.

The top federal prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said ‌at a press conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case ‌and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."

Advertisement

"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," he said. "Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they'll answer for it."

The Alaska contest is widely ​seen as one of the US Senate races that could sway control of the chamber, now narrowly held by Trump's Republicans.

TRUMP ORDERED SUIT, CLAIMS 'FRAUD AT HIGHEST LEVEL'

The Justice Department's legal actions in Alaska and California, where the Trump administration is trying to prevent some ballots from being counted, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution.

When the DOJ filed the civil suit against Alaska a week ago, Trump told reporters, "I'm the one that said do it."

Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the Alaska investigation proceed, although Trump has called for a ‌prosecution of Senate candidate Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

"This is voter fraud at the ⁠highest level," Trump told a Florida rally on Friday.

The Department of Justice asked a federal judge on Friday to ensure the preservation of ballots that "may be impacted by voter confusion." The court filing requested the judge's help obtaining documents from the Democratic campaign and others to determine "whether Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy is frivolous ⁠or fraudulent."

The DOJ also has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken. Both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.

If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, ​they ​intend to launch investigations of the Trump administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran.

The ​New York Times reported this week that staffers from the Peltola campaign and ‌the Democratic Party's Senate campaign arm helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr, a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village, to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not independently confirmed the Times' reporting.

Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.

SURGE OF VOTING NATIONWIDE DESPITE UNCERTAINTY

Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further disruptions from the Trump administration, which has sued about 30 states seeking unredacted voter rolls.

"The new tactic is just to create enough confusion and enough uncertainty and enough doubt through the filing of all these lawsuits to lay the groundwork to ultimately, I think, challenge the results once the dust settles after Tuesday," said Jonathan Diaz of the ‌nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center.

Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his ​2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies ​and investigations have found.

Despite any uncertainty, a record 49 million people have cast early ballots, ​more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot ‌by mail.

The DOJ has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing ​subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal ​probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.

A US appeals court on Friday rejected the department's request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.

A lower court judge had denied the ​administration's request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters.

Trump said ‌on Friday he would attend weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, a day after canceling them, telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called ​him and asked him to reconsider.

(Additional reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Nathan Layne, Jana Winter, Max Schwarz, Kia Johnson, Maria Tsvetkova, Doina Chiacu, Jan Wolfe and David Morgan; Writing ​by Joseph Ax and Daniel Trotta; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Scott Malone, Alistair Bell and Rosalba O'Brien)

data.title: DOJ warned election workers in all 50 states. Now a judge has stepped in.
data.description:
Judge orders DOJ to stop threatening to prosecute election officials

Josh Gerstein and Kyle Cheney
Updated Sat, October 31, 2026 at 1:05 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A federal judge on Friday ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution over their handling of disputes about voter qualifications.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson also ordered the Trump administration to cease demanding that election workers remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse to issue ballots to specific voters or segregate ballots cast in the midterms based on the administration's claims that some voters are ineligible.

"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote.

Advertisement

Thompson, a San Francisco-based Biden appointee, issued the temporary restraining order in connection with a lawsuit brought by the Service Employees International Union and other groups. Her directive also requires the DOJ to reach out to any state or local officials who received warnings about possible prosecution and inform them that "demands and threats of prosecution to election officials and workers … have been enjoined."

The Justice Department on Thursday sent letters to election workers in all 50 states alluding to possible prosecution if they didn't preserve election records. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the judge's broad ruling.

Thompson's order effectively enforces a stern warning issued to the Trump administration by another California-based federal judge, David Carter, earlier this week. "These threats must stop," Carter wrote in a ruling that threw out the Justice Department's effort to compel California to set aside any ballots cast by up to 20,000 people federal officials had identified as likely noncitizens. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday declined to set aside Carter's order.

Thompson's new directive also follows an order by U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, chief of the federal district court in Washington, D.C., to require the Trump administration to provide the list of those 20,000 purported noncitizens to an immigrant advocacy group. Boasberg's order was rooted, in part, on the group's claim that the Trump administration's threats were influencing the conduct of state and local elected officials.

data.title: Abdul El-Sayed leads Michigan Senate polls, but a divide among Dems could hurt him
data.description:
Abdul El-Sayed vs. Mike Rogers: Who has a better chance of winning Michigan's marquee Senate battle?

The race, which has been rocked by controversy, could decide which party controls the Senate.

Andrew Romano, Mike Bebernes
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 5:17 PM UTC
9 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

On Election Day, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will face off in what may be the marquee battle of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan. 

It's a contest that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate. 

Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who caucus with them. They need 51 to win back the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.) Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible, but Democrats are also playing defense in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan. The Great Lakes State looks like the closest of the three. 

Advertisement

Democrats are pinning their hopes on El-Sayed, an unapologetic 41-year-old progressive who's pushing policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel; who's willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment; and who's vying to become America's first Muslim senator.

Republicans have handed the reins to Rogers, a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran.

The race has been rocked by several controversies, including the revelation this week that the fiancé of Rep. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, will not join her in voting for El-Sayed due to his frequent criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza. 

"Every time [El-Sayed] talks about genocide, Jews get death threats," Stevens's fiancé, a Michigan lawyer and registered Democrat named Jason Turkish, claimed Wednesday at a Rogers campaign event. "We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul."

The Associated Press reported Thursday that Stevens — who has urged El-Sayed to reach out to her supporters — will campaign with him this weekend. It'll be their first time appearing together since August.

Further raising the stakes is the fact that Michigan couldn't be more purple, having swung to Trump in 2016, then Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, then back to Trump in 2024 — always by slim margins. 

Here's everything you need to know about the Michigan Senate contest.

Who's winning? Here's what the polls say.

Twelve polls have been conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed with leads ranging from 1 to 7 percentage points. New surveys from both CBS Detroit and CNN give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. The only recent poll to show Rogers ahead (by 2 points) was sponsored by a group affiliated with the former congressman.

To close the gap on Election Day, Rogers has been reaching out to two groups who backed Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary: Black and Jewish Democrats. 

In August, Stevens won a majority of Michigan's large counties with significant Black populations by an average of 8.5 percentage points. She also won Detroit with more than 60% of the vote, making El-Sayed the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city. 

Some members of Michigan's Jewish community also gravitated toward Stevens because El-Sayed has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump." 

"Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April. "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both."

It remains to be seen whether Rogers's outreach will pay off; he's also targeting more reliable Republican constituencies such as the nearly 4 million Michiganders ages 50 and older. So far, polls suggest that El-Sayed's strategy — trying to maximize his support among anti-establishment voters, Arab Americans and young voters — has put him ahead in the polls. 

But the polls have overestimated El-Sayed before. In the run-up to August's primary, several surveys showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. The race ended up being much closer than expected, with El-Sayed edging Stevens by less than 1 percentage point. 

How controversial has the race been? 

El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists." 

Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed without evidence that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith. 

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After Trump referred to El-Sayed as "Mohammed" — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style. 

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Sunday. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker, a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American. 

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies. 

An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf. 

"They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks.

"No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."

Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it. 

"That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now."

Who is El-Sayed? 

El-Sayed, 41, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science. 

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department. 

In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis. He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists.

Who is Rogers? 

Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. He earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress. 

Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes. During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as "the economic and national security danger posed by China." 

Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN.

Rogers returned to run for the Senate in 2024. Roughly six months after that loss, he announced his plan to run again in 2026. 

Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues — including abortion, immigration and transgender rights — but his opinion on Trump has shifted through the years. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has retreated from his early support for the president on two key issues: calling for Trump to end the "tariff war" with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should also "end quickly."

Washoe County election workers test voting machines ahead of the 2026 midterm elections in Reno

Washoe County election workers test voting machines ahead of the 2026 midterm elections in Reno, Nevada, US, October 7, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Elizabeth Mendez/File Photo

By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Frandino

The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, ‌said at a press conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the ‌case and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."

"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," he said. "Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they'll answer for it."

Separately, the department on Friday ​asked a federal judge to block Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, also named Daniel Sullivan.

The contest between Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is widely seen as one of the few Senate races that could sway control of the chamber on November 3.

If Democrats cannot flip the seat, their path to a majority narrows considerably, with the party needing to win at least two other races in mostly Republican states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. Trump's fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the US House of Representatives, ⁠according to nonpartisan analysts.

The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party's Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times' reporting.

Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has ​also ​denied involvement. Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.

It is not clear what, if any, laws ​may have been broken; both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known ‌candidates to siphon votes from their opponents. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted.

Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the investigation proceed. He also said the probe had been ongoing for months and that the Times report had added urgency to the investigation, but did not explain how.

Peltola's campaign has asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department's lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis.

CALIFORNIA PROBE

The Justice Department has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.

A US appeals court on Friday rejected the department's request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the ‌Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.

A lower court judge had ​already denied the administration's request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters. California officials have said the Justice ​Department's assertions relied on suspect data.

The administration's legal moves represent an extraordinary federal intervention in ​state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington.

Trump has ‌long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that ​his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was ​the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.

The president will campaign on Friday in Florida, the latest in a series of rallies he has headlined in states he won handily in 2024 but where Democrats are now competitive, as he tries to stave off Republican losses on Tuesday.

Trump said on Friday he would attend weekend ​rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a day after canceling them, ‌telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 ​election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday.

(Additional reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Nathan Layne, Jana Winter, Max Schwarz, Kia Johnson, Maria Tsvetkova, Doina Chiacu and Jan Wolfe; Writing ​by Joseph Ax and Jonathan Allen; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Scott Malone, Alistair Bell and Rosalba O'Brien)

data.title: Criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate in Alaska
data.description:
Top federal prosecutor in Alaska says criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate

ALANNA DURKIN RICHER, JOSHUA GOODMAN and BECKY BOHRER
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 8:25 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Election 2026 Alaska

1 of 3
A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Haven Daley) (AP Photo/Haven Daley)

ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal investigation related to an alleged scheme to confuse voters by putting a Senate candidate on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent.

The investigation has been ongoing for several months, but revelations this week from The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska," U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters.

"When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information to deceive voters and we will act on it. We are acting on it intensely and swiftly," Heyman said.

Advertisement

Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but encouraged the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.

Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot, where Peltola is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"I just want to clear the air," she said at a campaign rally at a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska's capital. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.

Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign. "Zero, none, zilch," he said in June after announcing his run.

The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber.

Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

State attorneys have asked a court to rule on the Justice Department's lawsuit by Monday, saying the case could "cast a cloud over Alaska's election that is contrary to the public interest."

Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting "reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska's elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes."

"Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections," Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting "substantially supports" earlier findings by the state's elections board into the matter.

Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. "Well, you're going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run."

___

Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau, Alaska.

data.title: Federal appeals court again denies Trump admin request to block 20,000 California ballots
data.description:
9th Circuit again denies Trump administration request to block 20,000 California ballots

Kevin Rector, Brittny Mejia
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 7:16 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A federal appeals court for the second time Friday denied a Trump administration request to block 20,000 ballots from California voters the administration alleges may be noncitizens — ruling that the administration had failed to show that "such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law."

The three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — ruled 2-1 that the U.S. Constitution gives the state and Congress the power to decide how elections are run, and that allowing the Trump administration to "misuse" federal statutes to "prescribe" how California must process ballots would "override the plain and manifest dictates of the Constitution itself."

"Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the Elections Clause to override California's established laws for challenging ballots or removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature's statutory scheme remains the only method to do so," the judges found.

Advertisement

The panel's majority — comprised of Trump appointee Mark J. Bennett and Biden appointee Gabriel P. Sanchez — wrote that "if the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts."

They also wrote that separate federal law prescribes sweeping changes to voter lists 90 days prior to an election, especially given questions about the reliability of the Trump administration's list of purported noncitizens.

"The suspect reliability of these lists found by the district court reflects the concern Congress sought to mitigate with the 90-day quiet period," they wrote.

Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, the other Trump appointee on the panel, dissented — arguing that his colleagues erred in denying a basic request by the Trump administration to ensure only citizens are voting.

"The federal government proposes a modest remedy — stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens," Bumatay wrote. "This solution would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens. The district court, and now our court, denies this reasonable request."

This article will be updated.

data.title: Renewed Iran war after midterms could threaten fragile U.S. gains in Hormuz
data.description:
A resumed Iran war after midterms would put fragile gains in Hormuz to the test

Susannah George, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 2:16 PM UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The United States is pointing to gains in the Strait of Hormuz, intent on demonstrating that weeks of complex and secretive military operations there have returned oil flows to near prewar levels and chipped away at a key piece of Iranian leverage ahead of a threatened return to all-out war after the U.S. midterm elections next week.

An increase in vessel traffic and the small percentage of ships disabled by Iranian strikes are signals "clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway," read a statement this week from U.S. Central Command announcing that Brad Cooper, the head of the command, had visited the strait.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

But while U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf have welcomed the operations along with oil industry and shipping firms, serious questions remain about how sustainable they are in the face of escalating Iranian attacks, according to two people with knowledge of the matter and two Western officials based in the region, who like others interviewed for this report spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive information. Also unclear, they said, is whether the U.S. military would be able to maintain the operations in the strait at the same time as resumed heavy strikes on Iranian territory after the U.S. midterm elections, as President Donald Trump has threatened.

In addition to increasing the volume of strikes on shipping, Tehran also appears to have adjusted its targeting in recent weeks, increasingly taking aim at engine rooms to disable vessels rather than just damage them, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter, who is close to the shipping industry. United Nations data shows that two ships have sunk this month as a result of Iranian attacks.

The U.S. operations that have enabled the dramatic increase in oil exports are some of the most complex of the war, according to a European security official and the two people with knowledge of the matter. U.S. forces have integrated air defenses, fighter jets, drones and warships to protect vessels in layers as they pass through the waterway, running a harrowing gantlet of Iranian attacks far beyond what ordinary seafarers sign up to face on the job. The European security official likened the operations to creating "a bubble" that moves along the strait as vessels make the transit.

Iranian attacks have made this month the most violent in the waterway since the war began. At least 25 ships in the strait have been hit in October, according to data collected by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, a maritime monitoring body affiliated with the British military.

But oil exports have also surged during the same period. Figures vary, but maritime analytics firm Kpler found that average daily oil exports reached 14 million barrels for the week ending on Oct. 18, about 80 percent of prewar averages. The rebound has been remarkable: In July, daily averages over a seven-day period were as low as 7 million barrels. U.S. Central Command doesn't release daily averages, but it said that "since summer," oil exports through the strait had reached 1.5 billion barrels.

The U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division leads the mission and runs a joint operations center in the United Arab Emirates, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter.

The UAE Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the country's role in the Hormuz operations.

At least 30 ships per day have transited the strait so far this month, according to the two individuals with knowledge of the matter. U.S. Central Command has released little information publicly about efforts to protect shipping in the strait, but it said Sunday that over the past six months, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the waterway.

Speaking about his visit to the strait in a social media video Friday, Cooper said he saw a resumption of shipping but no signs of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "When I flew over the strait, I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting, all types - cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas," he said. "I didn't see the IRGC out there at all."

The resumption of traffic through the strait - which nearly ceased amid the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran - has brought a critical lifeline for U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf as well as the shipping and energy industries. "Everyone wanted this," said the second person with knowledge of the matter, who is in contact with industry leaders and government officials. But that person cautioned that the private sector and U.S. allies in the region view the effort as an imperfect, temporary measure. The two Western officials based in the region said they have heard similar concerns about the operations in the strait.

Since U.S. operations ramped up in August, seven seafarers have been killed and 18 injured, according to United Nations data. The risk levels are currently so high that nearly all the vessels willing to make the trip are state owned and operated. Most private companies continue to refuse to use the strait even under U.S. protection, according to the individuals and officials.

"The situation is completely unsustainable," said one of the Western officials based in the region. While vessel traffic has increased for oil exports, the official said, few vessels carrying liquefied natural gas have taken the risk. "If one of those gets hit, it's not just an oil spill; it's an explosion," the official said.

The fact that Iran has escalated attacks on shipping is itself a demonstration of U.S. successes in the waterway, according to Gregory Brew, an energy and Iran analyst at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy firm.

"The U.S. has achieved something pretty considerable, overcoming Iran's closure of the strait earlier this year, but it's not enough," he said, referring to energy prices that have remained high despite increases to traffic.

Iran has demonstrated that it doesn't need to completely close the waterway to keep prices high, but the U.S. has found that even partially reopening the strait isn't moving energy markets the desired amount, according to Brew. "As long as it's contested, then Iran is achieving their objective," he said.

But Kevin Donegan, a retired vice admiral who served in Bahrain as the commander of the Navy's Fifth Fleet, said he sees the operations differently. Compared with the escort operations of the "tanker wars" in the 1980s, current U.S. operations have a smaller footprint and are more nimble, he said.

"During the tanker wars, ships were lining up and being escorted with lots of naval vessels, big convoys," he said. "We'd brute-force them through in groups. That's not what's happening now."

Donegan said he couldn't share further details of the operations, but he described them as "a piece of maritime superiority" that can be turned on and off and moved to where vessels are most vulnerable.

"Think of it as a moving sanctuary," he said.

Every day, the vessels registered to make the crossing assemble off the coast of the United Arab Emirates and are delivered guidelines to follow, including the instruction to turn off the Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders that broadcast the vessel's location with satellite and radio signals. The vessels are then given coordinates marking the safe passageway, with labeled checkpoints denoted by the NATO phonetic alphabet.

Once the vessels have exited the strait, they transfer their cargo to privately owned ships in the Gulf of Oman before traveling back to the Persian Gulf to load up again. Because so few vessels are willing to risk Iranian attacks, roughly the same group of vessels is making the trip back and forth from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.

"It's a de facto shadow fleet," said the Western official based in the region, using a term to describe vessels that attempt to evade sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil by switching off AIS and moving oil with ship-to-ship transfers.

Donegan, the retired vice admiral, said the operations also appear to be having a secondary function: They are beginning to build the framework of a future regional coalition to counter Iran. He cited support for the operations from the Emirati, Kuwaiti and Iraqi governments.

The Trump administration "has to continue to build this coalition of countries saying that what Iran's doing is not acceptable," he said.

"The way forward is to get the Iranians to a tipping point."
